policydecision_details: Brazil’s Second NDC (2024) aims to accelerate the transition towards a low-carbon, climate-resilient economy while promoting sustainable development, biodiversity conservation and climate justice. It establishes a binding national commitment to reduce net greenhouse gas emissions by 59–67% by 2035 compared with 2005 levels, equivalent to 0.85–1.05 GtCO₂e, supporting the goal of climate neutrality by 2050. Key priorities include eliminating deforestation, restoring degraded ecosystems, expanding renewable energy, promoting low-carbon agriculture and livestock production, and strengthening climate adaptation and food security. The NDC highlights the Amazon restoration initiative, targeting 6 million hectares of forest restoration by 2030 and 24 million hectares by 2050. Implementation covers 2020–2035, coordinated through the National Climate Plan, including sectoral mitigation and adaptation strategies, supported by climate finance, technological innovation and international cooperation.

Bolivia’s NDC 3.0 establishes climate mitigation and adaptation commitments for 2026–2035, promoting low-carbon, climate-resilient development while strengthening food, water and energy security. It prioritizes sustainable forest management, renewable energy, climate-resilient agriculture, waste management and integrated water resource management. Key targets by 2035 include increasing strategic crop yields by at least 30% compared with 2019–2024, introducing sustainable livestock practices across 155,000 hectares, strengthening climate resilience for 400,000 agricultural producers, and achieving 25% municipal solid waste recovery. Additional commitments include implementing 102 water resource management plans and introducing water-efficient irrigation technologies across 653,981 hectares. Implementation spans 2026–2035, with many commitments conditional on international climate finance, technology transfer and capacity-building support.

policy_description: National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan – NBSAP 2025-2030 - Brazil
policydecision_details: Brazil’s National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan (NBSAP), published in 2025, establishes a comprehensive framework to halt biodiversity loss, restore degraded ecosystems and promote sustainable use of natural resources, aligned with the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. The strategy defines 25 national biodiversity targets for 2030, four long-term strategic objectives for 2050 and 234 implementation actions. Key quantitative commitments include achieving zero deforestation and conversion of native vegetation by 2030, placing at least 30% of degraded or altered areas in each biome and the coastal-marine system under effective restoration, and conserving and effectively managing at least 80% of the Amazon biome, 30% of each other biome and 30% of coastal and marine ecosystems by 2030. Priority interventions include sustainable agriculture, livestock production and fisheries, forest restoration, ecosystem protection, biodiversity-friendly production systems, bioeconomy development, pollution reduction, and the protection of Indigenous Peoples’ and local communities’ rights. Implementation is coordinated by the Ministry of the Environment and Climate Change, involving 20 ministries and 30 federal entities and agencies. The strategy also commits to developing and initiating a national biodiversity financing strategy by 2026, mobilising domestic and international public and private resources. However, no consolidated implementation budget or quantified national financing requirement is specified in the document.

policy_description: Estrategia Nacional de Biodiversidad y Plan de Acción 2025 - 2030
policydecision_details: El Salvador’s National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan (EPANB), published in March 2025, establishes a national framework to restore, conserve and sustainably use biodiversity while strengthening climate resilience, economic competitiveness and human well-being, in alignment with the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. The strategy defines 10 national targets, 24 strategic actions and 95 operational actions, organized around three pillars: ecosystem restoration and conservation, sustainable biodiversity management and integration of biodiversity into economic and social development. A key quantitative target is to effectively restore at least 10% of prioritized degraded natural ecosystems and agroecosystems by 2030. Priority measures include forest and mangrove restoration, protection of marine and freshwater ecosystems, improved management of protected areas, sustainable agriculture, livestock, fisheries and forestry, wildlife conservation, ecological connectivity and biodiversity-sensitive territorial planning. Implementation covers 2025–2030, led by the Ministry of Environment and Natural Resources in coordination with other government institutions, the private sector, civil society and local communities. The strategy estimates USD 493.54 million in implementation financing requirements, including approximately USD 212.19 million for sustainable agricultural, livestock, forestry and fisheries management, USD 175.03 million for ecosystem restoration, and USD 79.22 million for protected-area conservation.

policy_description: STRATÉGIE ET PLAN D’ACTION NATIONAUX POUR LA BIODIVERSITÉ 2025-2030 DE LA RÉPUBLIQUE DÉMOCRATIQUE DU CONGO
policydecision_details: The Democratic Republic of the Congo’s National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan (NBSAP), published in November 2025, establishes a comprehensive national framework to conserve, restore and sustainably use biodiversity while promoting inclusive socioeconomic development, aligned with the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. The strategy identifies 25 national biodiversity objectives organized around five strategic priorities: biodiversity conservation, ecosystem restoration, sustainable use and equitable benefit-sharing, economic valorization of biological resources, and inclusive governance and sustainable financing. Key quantitative targets include restoring at least 30% of degraded ecosystems and expanding effectively conserved and sustainably managed areas to at least 30% of national territory by 2030. Priority measures include forest and wetland restoration, threatened species protection, sustainable agriculture, fisheries and forestry, pollution reduction, biodiversity-sensitive land-use planning, and stronger participation of Indigenous Peoples and local communities. Implementation covers 2025–2030, with priority actions during 2025–2027 and broader implementation during 2028–2030, coordinated by the Ministry of Environment alongside sectoral ministries, provincial authorities and local stakeholders. The strategy estimates USD 379.5 million in financing requirements for priority actions, to be mobilized through national budgets, international environmental funds, private investment and innovative biodiversity financing mechanisms.

policy_description: Updated Belgian National Biodiversity Strategy for 2030
policydecision_details: Belgium’s Updated National Biodiversity Strategy for 2030, approved on 30 January 2025, aims to halt biodiversity loss, restore degraded ecosystems and integrate biodiversity conservation into national and regional policies. It establishes 16 strategic objectives and 82 operational objectives, covering ecosystem protection, sustainable agriculture, forestry and fisheries, pollution reduction and biodiversity-friendly production and consumption. Key targets include contributing to the protection of 30% of terrestrial and marine areas, with 10% of these areas strictly protected, and the restoration of at least 30% of degraded ecosystems by 2030. The strategy also promotes sustainable resource management, reduced food waste, biodiversity financing and stronger monitoring and institutional coordination. Implementation covers 2025–2030, involving federal and regional authorities, with progress monitored through national reports to the Convention on Biological Diversity and a long-term vision for 2050.

The Antibiotic Stewardship Manual provides a comprehensive technical and operational framework for improving antimicrobial use and combating antimicrobial resistance (AMR). The manual supports the implementation of Taiwan’s National Antibiotic Stewardship Programme, launched in 2013, which aims to improve patient safety and healthcare quality, reduce unnecessary antimicrobial consumption, prevent the emergence and transmission of multidrug-resistant microorganisms, and decrease healthcare-associated infections. Although it acknowledges the importance of a One Health approach, encompassing human, animal, food and environmental health, its operational recommendations primarily target healthcare institutions. The manual identifies four implementation strategies: antimicrobial resistance and antibiotic consumption surveillance, rational antimicrobial use, infection prevention and control, and institutional culture change. Key interventions include establishing multidisciplinary antimicrobial stewardship teams involving physicians, pharmacists, nurses, microbiologists and infection control specialists; developing evidence-based prescribing guidelines; strengthening microbiological laboratory diagnostics; monitoring antimicrobial consumption and resistance patterns; and implementing infection prevention measures, including hand hygiene, environmental disinfection and patient isolation. Additional priorities include integrating information technology into prescription monitoring, conducting internal audits and quality improvement assessments, and providing professional training and public awareness activities. Implementation is supported by a three-tier organizational structure comprising a national project management centre, seven demonstration centres and participating hospitals, with regular performance evaluations and knowledge-sharing activities

policy_description: Prioritised Action Framework (PAF) for the Natura 2000 Network in Poland
policydecision_details: The Prioritized Action Framework (PAF) for Natura 2000 in Poland for the Multiannual Financial Framework 2021–2027 (Priorytetowe Ramy Działań dla sieci Natura 2000 w Polsce) establishes a national strategic framework for financing biodiversity conservation, habitat restoration, and sustainable management of protected areas. Prepared under Article 8 of the EU Habitats Directive (92/43/EEC), the framework identifies priority conservation measures and their estimated financing needs for the 2021–2027 period. Its main objective is to maintain or restore the favourable conservation status of natural habitats and protected species, strengthen the ecological coherence of the Natura 2000 network, and integrate biodiversity protection into agricultural, forestry, fisheries, and regional development policies. The framework is coordinated by Poland's General Directorate for Environmental Protection. The framework prioritizes habitat restoration, species conservation, sustainable agricultural and forest management, wetland protection, and biodiversity monitoring. Key interventions include restoring peatlands, marshes and other wetlands; maintaining biodiversity-rich grasslands through appropriate mowing and grazing practices; conserving agricultural habitats and farmland-dependent species; improving forest habitat conditions; and restoring freshwater, coastal and marine ecosystems. Additional measures address the conservation of endangered species, management of protected areas, ecological research, environmental education, and stakeholder participation. Particular attention is given to integrating conservation measures into agricultural and rural development funding, including support through the European Agricultural Fund for Rural Development (EAFRD). Other financing instruments include the European Regional Development Fund, Cohesion Fund, European Maritime and Fisheries Fund, LIFE programme, and national environmental funds. The document identifies priority financial requirements and implementation arrangements for conservation measures across different habitat categories

policy_description: IV. Action Programme for the protection of waters from pollution caused by nitrates of agricultural origin
policydecision_details: The Fourth Action Programme for the Protection of Waters against Pollution Caused by Nitrates from Agricultural Sources (IV. Akcijski program zaštite voda od onečišćenja uzrokovanog nitratima poljoprivrednog podrijetla), adopted by Croatia’s Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries on 16 June 2025, establishes regulatory measures to prevent and reduce nitrate pollution from agricultural activities. Published on 27 June 2025, the programme entered into force on 1 July 2025 for a four-year period, replacing the Third Action Programme. Its primary objective is to protect surface water and groundwater quality by limiting agricultural nitrate pollution. The programme focuses on sustainable fertilizer management, manure storage, nutrient-use efficiency, and water pollution prevention. It establishes mandatory requirements for agricultural holdings located in designated nitrate-vulnerable zones, while recommending similar practices elsewhere. Key measures include limiting nitrogen application from livestock manure to 170 kg per hectare annually, establishing crop-specific nitrogen application limits, restricting fertilizer use during certain periods and on frozen, flooded, or waterlogged soils, and maintaining protective distances from water bodies. It also requires appropriate manure storage facilities with sufficient capacity for six months, periodic soil testing, and recordkeeping on fertilizer use. These measures aim to reduce nutrient runoff, protect aquatic ecosystems, and promote environmentally sustainable agricultural production.

policy_description: Opinions of the General Office of the CPC Central Committee and the General Office of the State Council on Promoting Green and Low-Carbon Transformation and Strengthening the Construction of the National Carbon Market.
policydecision_details: The Opinions on Promoting Green and Low-Carbon Transition and Strengthening the National Carbon Market, issued by the General Offices of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and the State Council on 24 May 2025 and published on 25 August 2025, establish a national policy framework to accelerate China's green transition, strengthen carbon pricing mechanisms, and support its carbon peaking and neutrality objectives. The policy aims to expand the national emissions trading system (ETS) to cover major industrial sectors by 2027 and establish a comprehensive carbon market based on total emissions caps and a combination of free and paid allowances by 2030. The policy focuses on greenhouse gas emission reductions, carbon trading, green finance, and low-carbon industrial transformation. Key priorities include expanding emissions trading to additional sectors and greenhouse gases, gradually shifting from emissions-intensity controls to absolute emissions caps, and strengthening voluntary carbon credit markets. It also promotes carbon finance instruments, improved emissions accounting and verification, digital monitoring systems, and stricter enforcement against emissions data manipulation. Additional measures encourage the use of certified emission reductions, strengthen institutional coordination, and promote international cooperation on carbon market standards and mechanisms under the Paris Agreement.

policy_description: Opinions of the General Office of the CPC Central Committee and the General Office of the State Council on Comprehensively Promoting the Protection and Management of Rivers.
policydecision_details: The Opinions on Comprehensively Advancing River Protection and Management, issued by the General Offices of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and the State Council on 17 June 2025, establish a national policy framework to strengthen water security, improve river basin management, and promote the sustainable use and conservation of water resources. By 2035, the policy aims to establish a modern flood prevention and disaster mitigation system, improve water-use efficiency and water supply security, and restore the ecological health of rivers and aquatic ecosystems. The policy focuses on integrated water resources management, flood prevention, water conservation, ecosystem restoration, and climate resilience. Key priorities include upgrading flood protection infrastructure, strengthening hydrological monitoring and early warning systems, expanding water-efficient irrigation, improving agricultural water productivity, and modernizing rural water supply networks. It also promotes groundwater protection, restoration of degraded rivers and wetlands, biodiversity conservation, pollution control, and wastewater management. Additional measures strengthen river basin governance, water pricing mechanisms, ecological compensation schemes, and digital monitoring technologies to support coordinated and sustainable water management.

policy_description: Opinions on Combating Illegal Fishing Activities and Strengthening Port State Inspections and Management of Foreign Fishing Vessels.
policydecision_details: The Opinions on Combating Illegal Fishing Activities and Strengthening Port State Inspections and Management of Foreign Fishing Vessels, jointly issued by six Chinese government authorities on 11 August 2025, establish a national framework to combat illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing, strengthen fisheries governance, and promote the sustainable use of marine resources. The policy supports China's implementation of the FAO Agreement on Port State Measures (PSMA), aimed at preventing illegally caught fish from entering domestic and international markets. The policy focuses on strengthening port inspections, preventing illegal fishing, improving fisheries monitoring, and enhancing international cooperation. Key measures include requiring foreign fishing vessels to use designated ports, submit entry notifications at least seven days before arrival, and undergo inspections covering at least 5% of authorized incoming vessels. Vessels involved in IUU fishing may be denied port entry or access to port services, while illegal catches, equipment, and proceeds may be confiscated. The policy also strengthens interagency coordination, information sharing, enforcement capacities, and cooperation with international fisheries management organizations to ensure compliance with international obligations.

policy_description: Contribución Determinada a Nivel Nacional (NDC) de Chile - (Actualización 2025)
policydecision_details: The Updated Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) of Chile 2025–2035, approved by the Ministry of the Environment through Supreme Decree No. 28 of 7 August 2025 and published on 20 September 2025, establishes a national framework to strengthen climate change mitigation and adaptation under the Paris Agreement. Building on Chile's 2020 NDC and its Framework Law on Climate Change (Law No. 21,455), it reaffirms the country's commitment to achieving greenhouse gas emissions neutrality by 2050 and promoting low-carbon, climate-resilient development. The NDC focuses on reducing greenhouse gas emissions, strengthening climate resilience, improving water security, and protecting biodiversity and natural carbon sinks. Key priorities include accelerating emissions reductions, promoting sustainable land use, restoring forests and peatlands, protecting marine and terrestrial ecosystems, and implementing nature-based solutions. Particular attention is given to climate adaptation in vulnerable sectors, including agriculture and water resources, through improved climate risk management and ecosystem restoration. The NDC includes 14 mitigation commitments, 6 adaptation commitments, and 12 integrated mitigation and adaptation commitments, alongside measures for climate finance, technology transfer, capacity building, and subnational climate governance.

policy_description: National Strategic Plan for Water and Sanitation (PLENAS 2.0)
policydecision_details: The National Strategic Water and Sanitation Plan 2.0 (Plano Estratégico Nacional de Água e Saneamento – PLENAS 2.0), approved by the Government of Cabo Verde through Resolution No. 52/2025 of 24 June 2025, establishes a national framework to achieve universal access to safe drinking water and sanitation services by 2030, while strengthening the efficiency, sustainability, and climate resilience of water infrastructure. The plan focuses on expanding water supply and wastewater treatment infrastructure, improving water-use efficiency, and ensuring affordable and reliable services, particularly in underserved rural communities. Its four strategic pillars address service effectiveness, efficiency, sustainability, and value creation, encompassing 20 strategic objectives and 54 operational measures. Key priorities include reducing water losses, promoting wastewater reuse, improving energy efficiency in desalination facilities, integrating renewable energy, and strengthening resilience to droughts and climate change. The plan also promotes social tariffs for vulnerable households, institutional coordination, digitalization, and sustainable financing, with estimated investment needs of CVE 32–70 billion.

Australia’s Net Zero Plan (2025) presents a comprehensive national strategy to achieve net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050, with an interim target of reducing emissions by 62–70% below 2005 levels by 2035. The Plan is legislated under the Climate Change Act 2022. It is structured into four parts: the climate change context, Australia’s emissions pathway, enabling policies and institutions, and collaborative efforts across society. The Plan outlines five decarbonisation priorities: clean electricity, electrification and efficiency, clean fuels, technology acceleration, and carbon removals. These priorities are supported by sector-specific strategies for electricity and energy, transport, industry, resources, agriculture and land, and the built environment. The plan emphasizes the importance of maintaining economic growth, attracting investment, and ensuring a fair and inclusive transition, particularly for First Nations communities and regions most affected by industrial change. The electricity sector is central to the transition. The Circular Economy Framework aims to double circularity by 2035, contributing to emissions reductions through improved resource efficiency. Clean fuels are being developed for sectors that cannot easily electrify, including heavy industry and long-distance transport. The government is investing in renewable hydrogen and in low-carbon liquid fuel production. Technology acceleration is supported through ARENA, the CEFC, and the Future Made in Australia Innovation Fund. Carbon removals are being scaled through land-based methods and emerging technologies. The ACCU Scheme and Safeguard Mechanism provide flexible, cost-effective pathways for emissions reduction, while voluntary markets and the Nature Repair Market support broader participation. Australia is also strengthening supply chains and trade relationships to support clean energy exports and reduce reliance on fossil fuels. First Nations leadership is integral to the plan. The First Nations Clean Energy Strategy supports self-determination, cultural protection, and equitable access to clean energy. Community engagement is emphasized throughout the plan. The Net Zero Economy Authority supports regions undergoing industrial transition, and initiatives such as the Developer Rating Scheme and Community Benefit Principles ensure that local communities are involved and benefit from the transition. Land-based abatement is being balanced with agricultural productivity and biodiversity goals, supported by improved data and planning.

The National Adaptation Plan outlines Australia’s strategic response to the increasing risks posed by climate change, drawing on the findings of the National Climate Risk Assessment (NCRA). It presents a comprehensive framework for coordinated national action across government, industry, and communities to build resilience and reduce vulnerability to climate hazards. The document begins by acknowledging the deep-rooted history of adaptation in Australia, particularly among First Nations peoples, and highlights the urgency of addressing climate risks that are already affecting communities, ecosystems, and infrastructure. The NCRA provides a detailed analysis of climate hazards under warming scenarios of 1.5°C, 2°C, and 3°C, identifying 11 priority risks across seven key systems: economy, infrastructure, natural environment, primary industries, health and social support, communities, and defence. The Plan sets out a vision for a well-adapted Australia, supported by targeted, evidence-based, and collaborative principles. It emphasises the importance of enabling adaptation through leadership, governance, and access to reliable climate data. Specific chapters address the unique vulnerabilities and adaptation needs of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, and detail sectoral strategies for economic resilience, infrastructure planning, environmental conservation, food and water security, public health, and disaster preparedness. The Plan also outlines current government initiatives, including significant investments in climate resilience, adaptation programs, and legislative reforms. It commits to developing a monitoring, evaluation, and learning system to track progress and inform future adaptation cycles. The document concludes by reinforcing the need for inclusive, place-based approaches and ongoing collaboration across jurisdictions to ensure Australia is equipped to face the challenges of a changing climate.

policy_description: Concept of Environmental Security for the period up to 2040
policydecision_details: The Order Approving the Implementation Rules for the Intervention “Management of the Spread of Invasive Species on Drainage Ditch Slopes” under Lithuania’s CAP Strategic Plan 2023–2027, adopted by the Minister of Agriculture on 9 April 2025 (Order No. 3D-208), establishes the eligibility conditions, financial support mechanisms, and implementation requirements for controlling invasive plant species along agricultural drainage ditches and regulated watercourses. The intervention aims to halt biodiversity loss, improve ecosystem services, and preserve agricultural habitats and landscapes, contributing to the environmental objectives of Lithuania’s Common Agricultural Policy Strategic Plan 2023–2027. The measure provides annual compensatory payments of EUR 644 per hectare, increased to EUR 773 per hectare when activities are implemented through partnership agreements. Eligible applicants are active farmers, individually or in cooperation with other landholders, drainage system associations or municipalities, managing at least 0.1 hectares of designated land. Beneficiaries must undertake five-year commitments to remove invasive plants through mowing, excavation or other prescribed methods, clear vegetation from drainage ditch slopes and adjacent three-metre maintenance strips, and prevent the use of fertilizers and livestock grazing in treated areas. Implementation is administered by the National Paying Agency, with annual applications, monitoring, photographic evidence and compliance controls to ensure effective eradication of invasive species.

Türkiye’s Second Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0) sets out a clear vision for addressing the country’s climate challenges while balancing economic growth and social equity. With 2035 as the target year, the policy commits to reducing greenhouse gas emissions by 466 million tonnes of CO₂ equivalent compared to the business-as-usual scenario, limiting total GHG emissions to 643 million tonnes. Türkiye’s target covers all Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) sectors, including energy, industrial processes and product use, agriculture, waste, and LULUCF. This milestone builds on Türkiye’s earlier pledge of a 41% reduction by 2030 and aligns with its long-term ambition of achieving net-zero emissions by 2053. The framework emphasizes fairness and ambition in light of national circumstances, aiming to strengthen resilience across all sectors while ensuring a just and inclusive transition that supports vulnerable groups, promotes sustainable development, and contributes to global climate goals. Türkiye’s Second NDC is backed by comprehensive legislation, long-term strategies, and inclusive governance. It balances mitigation, adaptation, social equity, and economic growth, positioning Türkiye as a proactive actor in global climate action. The Climate Change Mitigation Strategy and Action Plan (2024–2030) outlines measures such as scaling up renewable energy, electrification, energy efficiency, and circular economy practices, while the Adaptation Strategy and Action Plan targets resilience in water, agriculture, health, biodiversity, and infrastructure. The Climate Law of 2025 provides the legal foundation for a national Emissions Trading System, a Green Taxonomy aligned with the EU, and mandatory Local Climate Action Plans across provinces. Complementary initiatives include industrial decarbonization roadmaps, hydrogen and mobility strategies, waste management reforms, and empowerment programs for women and youth. Together, these actions form an integrated pathway that mobilizes finance, technology, and social participation to ensure Türkiye’s transition toward a low-carbon, climate-resilient future.

Pakistan’s NDC 3.0 presents an ambitious, economy-wide framework aimed at simultaneously reducing greenhouse gas emissions and strengthening national resilience in the face of intensifying climate risks. Despite contributing minimally to global emissions, Pakistan ranks among the most climate-vulnerable countries, experiencing accelerated glacial melt, catastrophic floods, extreme heat, shifting monsoon patterns, and sea-level rise. The updated NDC aligns with national development priorities and global climate commitments, outlining a voluntary 50% emissions-reduction target by 2035—17% through domestic measures and 33% conditional on grant-based international support. The plan integrates mitigation actions across energy, transport, industry, agriculture, waste, and forestry, supported by major shifts toward renewable energy, energy efficiency, clean mobility, and large-scale ecosystem restoration. Adaptation stands as the central pillar of the NDC, reflecting Pakistan’s acute exposure to climate hazards and the socio-economic vulnerabilities embedded in agriculture, water resources, public health, and urban systems. Guided by the National Adaptation Plan (2023), the document emphasizes climate-resilient infrastructure, improved water management, ecosystem rehabilitation, disaster-risk reduction, and strengthened early-warning systems. Cross-cutting priorities include gender equality, youth engagement, social inclusion, and a just transition that protects workers and communities affected by the shift to a low-carbon economy.

The Nationally Determined Contribution of Nicaragua (2025) (Contribución Nacionalmente Determinada de Nicaragua) establishes the country's updated framework for climate change mitigation and adaptation under the Paris Agreement. Building on the National Climate Change Policy (2022) and the National Plan to Combat Poverty and Promote Human Development 2022–2026, the document aims to promote low-carbon, climate-resilient and inclusive development, while strengthening food security, protecting natural resources and reducing vulnerability to climate-related hazards. In 2022, Nicaragua's net greenhouse gas emissions amounted to approximately 28.79 million tonnes of CO₂ equivalent, with agriculture, forestry and other land use accounting for 64.44% of total emissions. The document presents mitigation scenarios for 2030, including an enhanced-ambition scenario projecting a 10% reduction compared with business-as-usual emissions. The NDC prioritizes renewable energy, sustainable forest management, climate-resilient agriculture, water security, biodiversity conservation and disaster risk reduction. Key mitigation commitments include increasing renewable energy to 65% of installed electricity generation capacity by 2030, conditional on international financing, and reducing emissions from gross deforestation by 25% by 2030 relative to the 2005–2015 reference period. Additional measures address industrial emissions and the progressive reduction of fluorinated gases. Agricultural and rural adaptation priorities include expanding water harvesting and irrigation systems in the Dry Corridor, promoting climate-resilient agricultural technologies, restoring forests and degraded ecosystems, strengthening watershed management, and improving farmers' adaptive capacities. The strategy also emphasizes modernizing hydrometeorological monitoring, strengthening early warning systems, improving water and sanitation infrastructure, and protecting vulnerable communities. Implementation depends on coordinated national institutions, community participation, international climate finance, technology transfer and capacity building.

This Mongolia’s Third Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0) strengthens its climate ambition under the Paris Agreement, aiming to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 30.3% unconditionally and up to 52.8% conditionally by 2035 compared to a business-as-usual scenario. The NDC focuses on transitioning from coal-based energy—currently supplying 90% of electricity—to renewable sources, improving energy efficiency, and promoting low-carbon technologies in transport, industry, and construction. Additional measures include restoring degraded rangelands, enhancing forest carbon sequestration, and introducing smart livestock and crop management practices. Mongolia also commits to achieving net-zero emissions by 2050, aligning with its Vision-2050 and Long-Term Low Emission Development Strategy. Adaptation priorities address vulnerabilities in water resources, biodiversity, forests, agriculture, health, and disaster risk reduction. Actions include expanding protected areas, improving water security through advanced technologies, and strengthening early warning systems. Social inclusion, gender equality, and climate education are integrated across all sectors.

policy_description: Second Nationally Determined Contribution Republic of Indonesia
policydecision_details: The Second Nationally Determined Contribution (Second NDC) of the Republic of Indonesia (2025) establishes the country's updated climate commitments under the Paris Agreement for the 2031–2035 period. Building on its Enhanced NDC, Indonesia adopts absolute greenhouse gas emission-level targets, using 2019 as the reference year, and maintains its long-term objective of achieving net-zero emissions by 2060 or sooner. The strategy covers five sectors: energy, industrial processes and product use, waste, agriculture, and forestry and other land use (FOLU). It projects emissions of approximately 1.26–1.49 billion tonnes of CO₂ equivalent by 2035, depending on the mitigation scenario, and aligns climate action with national development priorities, including food, water and energy security. The Second NDC prioritizes low-emission agriculture, sustainable forest management, ecosystem restoration, renewable energy, and climate adaptation. Agricultural measures seek to reduce greenhouse gas emissions while strengthening the resilience of farming systems and rural livelihoods. Forestry interventions emphasize reducing deforestation and forest degradation, restoring degraded ecosystems, protecting carbon stocks and expanding sustainable forest management. Adaptation priorities include strengthening food and water security, improving disaster risk management, and protecting coastal and marine ecosystems. Implementation relies on coordinated national and subnational planning, carbon pricing instruments, climate finance, technology transfer, capacity building and enhanced monitoring and reporting systems. The document estimates that approximately USD 472.6 billion in investment will be required to achieve its climate targets.

policy_description: Contribution Déterminée au niveau National (CDN 3.0 ) de la République de Guinée
policydecision_details: This Second Nationally Determined Contribution (SNDC) represents Indonesia’s continued commitment to integrate the country's climate targets with the international obligations and the national development Plan. This Second Nationally Determined Contribution maintains Indonesia's climate ambition to achieve Net Zero Emissions by 2060 and covers the following sectors: energy, industrial processes and product use, waste, agriculture, forestry and other land use. The Contribution is structured as follows: national context, general policies and long-term strategy on low carbon and climate resilience; mitigation measures; adaptation measures; information to facilitate clarity, transparency and understanding: quantifiable information on the reference point and time frames and periods for implementation, scope and coverage, planning processes, methodological approach, Indonesia's contributes towards achieving the objective of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change; National Registry System as the backbone of the enhanced transparency framework; financial and technological means of implementation, capacity building. Concerning adaptation measures, the Contribution updates the country's policy direction through a range of strategic programmes and actions aimed at strengthening resilience in economic, social, livelihood, ecosystem, and landscape systems. The Contribution also integrates adaptation and mitigation efforts by identifying adaptation actions that also deliver greenhouse gas mitigation co-benefits, supported by research and pilot projects, and by strengthening the importance of including harvested wood products in the measurement and reporting of the SNDC progresses. Further actions analysed by this Contribution include: improvements in the national registry system, by integrating systems related to climate change, and the development of a national carbon registry linked to the Indonesia Stock Exchange; management and mobilisation of funds for environmental and climate initiatives. The Contribution is also based on the following nine programmes: building ownership and commitment among Ministries and other governmental institutions; capacity building and enhancing capacity of institutions and human resources at all levels; creating enabling environment to engage wider stakeholders in mitigation and adaptation measures as well as in resource mobilisation; developing framework and network for coordination and building synergy among sectors, regions and actors; supporting the implementation of transparency framework at the national level with one greenhouse gas emissions data policy; developing policies, planning and intervention programmes, including integrating mitigation and adaptation measures into development planning, to secure financial support and facilitate resource mobilisation; monitoring and reviewing the Contribution.

Eswatini’s Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0) outlines an enhanced climate strategy for 2027–2035. The Country aims to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 2.24 MtCO₂eq by 2035 relative to the business-as-usual scenario, with 31% of reductions financed domestically and the remainder contingent on international support. The energy sector, the largest emitter, is central to mitigation efforts through renewable energy expansion, clean cooking solutions, energy efficiency, and low-carbon transport initiatives. Additional measures target waste management, industrial processes, and agriculture, forestry, and land use (AFOLU), including landscape restoration and carbon sequestration through forest rehabilitation and tree planting. Adaptation is prioritized due to Eswatini’s vulnerability to rising temperatures, erratic rainfall, droughts, floods, and tropical storms. Seven sectors—agriculture, water, health, energy, disaster risk reduction, ecosystems and biodiversity, and infrastructure—form the core of adaptation actions. These include climate-smart agriculture, improved irrigation, resilient health systems, water governance reforms, and climate-proof infrastructure. Ecosystem restoration and biodiversity conservation are emphasized to enhance resilience and maintain ecological integrity. Cross-cutting measures integrate gender equality, youth participation, and social inclusion, ensuring that climate actions are equitable and aligned with Just Transition principles. The NDC also introduces a robust climate finance architecture, leveraging domestic resources, green bonds, and carbon markets. Technology transfer and capacity building are identified as critical enablers, alongside strengthening monitoring, reporting, and verification systems to comply with the Enhanced Transparency Framework.

policy_description: Contributions Déterminées au Niveau National CDN 3.0
policydecision_details: The Updated Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0) of Côte d’Ivoire, published in October 2025, establishes a national framework to strengthen climate change mitigation and adaptation under the Paris Agreement. Building on previous NDC commitments, it aims to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 33.07% by 2035 compared with the business-as-usual scenario, while pursuing long-term carbon neutrality and promoting inclusive, climate-resilient development. The NDC focuses on greenhouse gas emission reductions, climate-resilient agriculture, sustainable forest management, water security, biodiversity conservation, and ecosystem restoration. Key priorities include reducing deforestation, promoting climate-smart agricultural practices, strengthening resilience to droughts and floods, improving water resources management, and accelerating the transition to renewable energy and low-carbon technologies. It also emphasizes nature-based solutions, gender equality, social inclusion, and a just transition, supported by climate finance, institutional coordination, technology transfer, and monitoring and reporting mechanisms.

Cambodia’s Third Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0) reaffirms the country’s strengthened climate ambition, integrating mitigation, adaptation, and enabling measures across key sectors. It emphasizes climate-resilient development to safeguard communities, ecosystems, and economic growth from increasing climate risks such as floods, droughts, heat waves, and sea-level rise. The NDC outlines deepened mitigation targets across energy, transport, agriculture, forestry, and waste, supported by expanded governance, capacity building, and inclusive stakeholder engagement, aiming to cut greenhouse gas emissions by 16% unconditionally and 55% conditionally by 2035 compared to the BAU scenario. Key mitigation actions include scaling renewable energy to 72–80%, phasing out coal, promoting electric mobility, reducing clinker in cement, and halving deforestation by 2030. Adaptation priorities span health, WASH, infrastructure, livelihoods, disaster risk management, social protection, food systems, and air quality. Importantly, it introduces social protection, social services, and child protection as adaptation sectors for the first time, recognizing the disproportionate climate impacts on vulnerable populations. The NDC emphasizes inclusivity, integrating gender equality, youth, Indigenous Peoples, and persons with disabilities, and aligns with SDGs. The NDC also underscores the importance of food systems and nutrition in climate resilience. It commits to shifting consumption towards healthier, more nutritious, and sustainable diets by improving access to diverse foods, regulating unhealthy and ultra-processed products, and strengthening links between nutrition and social protection—such as home-grown school feeding programs. The NDC further promotes reducing food loss and waste, supporting domestic fruit and vegetable production, and expanding fortified rice use to improve public health while contributing to Cambodia’s climate goals.

Belize’s Third Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0) strengthens climate ambition under the Paris Agreement, targeting both mitigation and adaptation. Despite being a net carbon sink and contributing minimally to global emissions, Belize faces severe climate risks as a Small Island Developing State (SIDS), including sea-level rise, coastal erosion, hurricanes, and droughts. NDC 3.0 sets enhanced targets for 2030 and new goals for 2035, aiming to avoid 6.2 MtCO₂e by 2035 through renewable energy expansion (75–80% of electricity from domestic sources), electric mobility adoption, waste management improvements, and increased carbon sequestration in agriculture and forestry. These efforts align with Belize’s Long-Term Low-Emissions Development Strategy (LT-LEDS) and net-zero vision for 2050. Adaptation is central to NDC 3.0, addressing vulnerabilities in coastal zones, water, agriculture, health, tourism, and infrastructure. Key actions include mangrove and coral reef restoration, ecosystem-based coastal protection, climate-smart agriculture, watershed conservation, and resilient housing policies. Health systems will integrate early warning for climate-sensitive diseases, while tourism and fisheries adopt sustainability standards. Gender equality and social inclusion are mainstreamed across all sectors.

This document presents the country’s updated climate commitments for the period 2025–2035 under the Paris Agreement. Barbados positions climate action as central to its national development trajectory, emphasizing that resilience, mitigation, and adaptation must advance together in a small island developing state highly exposed to climate impacts. The document outlines the country's enhanced ambition to align with the goal of limiting global warming to 1.5°C, building on the 2015 and 2021 NDCs and incorporating updated data, sectoral information, and improved methodologies. Barbados reaffirms that while its historical responsibility for global emissions is minimal, it remains committed to contributing its fair share to global climate efforts. The NDC details national circumstances that shape Barbados’ climate policy, including its geographical characteristics, reliance on tourism, high population density, and exposure to extreme weather events, sea-level rise, coastal erosion, drought, and flooding. These vulnerabilities demonstrate the urgency of coordinated adaptation and resilience measures. The country highlights the rising economic and social costs of climate change and stresses the importance of integrating adaptation into all sectors, including coastal protection, water management, agricultural systems, and public health. Barbados underscores that sustainable development and climate resilience are inseparable goals, particularly in the context of the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. At the core of its mitigation commitment, Barbados commits to an absolute 45% reduction of greenhouse gas emissions below 2008 levels by 2035, with conditional targets supported by international finance, technology transfer, and capacity building. The mitigation pathway prioritizes rapid decarbonization of the electricity sector, expansion of renewable energy—aiming for 95% renewables in electricity production by 2035—and substantial improvements in energy efficiency and electrification of transport. Additional contributions include reducing waste generation, improving landfill management with methane flaring, and phasing out clinker production. These measures align with updated projections and the Integrated Resource and Resilience Plan. Adaptation remains a national priority, reflecting the constraints and needs of a water-scarce and climate-vulnerable island. Key adaptation strategies include strengthening integrated coastal zone management, enhancing water reuse and groundwater protection, improving agricultural resilience, protecting coral reefs and mangroves, and supporting nature-based solutions. Barbados emphasizes that adaptation strategies require significant financing and international support to address the limits of national fiscal capacity, particularly given the country’s high debt burden. The NDC also outlines institutional and procedural components, including stakeholder engagement, transparency under the Enhanced Transparency Framework, and the need for improved monitoring, reporting, and verification systems. Barbados is expanding institutional capacity through initiatives such as the Capacity Building Initiative for Transparency and support from regional and international partners. The NDC stresses that climate ambition will depend on securing adequate climate finance, deploying innovative financial instruments, and reforming international financial systems to address the unique vulnerabilities of small island developing states. Overall, the Barbados 2025 Second NDC reflects a substantial increase in ambition and a comprehensive effort to integrate climate resilience, mitigation, and sustainable development.

Azerbaijan’s NDC 3.0 sets out an economy-wide decarbonization strategy that encompasses all major sectors contributing to greenhouse gas emissions. It establishes ambitious reduction targets across power, buildings, oil and gas, transportation, industry, waste, and Agriculture, Forestry, and Other Land Use (AFOLU) sectors, with the goal of reducing emissions by 40% by 2035 compared to 1990 levels. The Baseline year has been shifted from 2016 to 2022 for more precise projections. Beyond mitigation, the framework seeks to bolster economic resilience and safeguard environmental sustainability, positioning climate action as a driver of long-term national development. The NDC 3.0 outlines sector-specific mitigation plans and implementation roadmaps, highlighting the role of diverse stakeholders and the need for technological innovation. It lays out clear pathways, action plans, and enabling conditions designed to deliver measurable results. Financing is emphasized as a cornerstone, with both public and private investment, as well as international cooperation, deemed essential to mobilize resources at scale. By integrating these elements, Azerbaijan’s NDC 3.0 not only fulfills its Paris Agreement commitments but also reinforces national policies for sustainable growth and active participation in global climate action. Azerbaijan’s decarbonization strategy envisions a broad transformation of its energy and industrial systems. Central to this effort is the transition from gas-fired power plants, machine drives, and heat sources toward electrification powered by renewable energy, ensuring that clean electricity becomes the backbone of the economy. Alongside this shift, the country aims to replace high‑emission fuels with sustainable biofuels, reducing reliance on carbon‑intensive energy sources and fostering a more resilient fuel mix. Complementing these measures, Azerbaijan plans to modernize operations by upgrading processes and introducing new equipment designed to reduce emissions. Energy efficiency also plays a critical role, with abatement achieved through lowering consumption of high‑emission fuels and optimizing resource use.

Australia’s 2035 Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) sets an economy-wide target to reduce net greenhouse gas emissions by 62–70% below 2005 levels by 2035, implemented as an emissions budget for 2031–2035. This commitment aligns with the Paris Agreement and Australia’s legislated Climate Change Act 2022, which mandates consideration of independent advice from the Climate Change Authority. The target builds on the 2030 goal of a 43% reduction and net zero by 2050, representing a significant increase in ambition. It is supported by the Net Zero Plan and six sectoral emissions reduction plans covering electricity, transport, industry, agriculture and land, resources, and the built environment. The NDC reflects Australia’s response to accelerating climate impacts, including extreme weather events and economic risks, and positions the country to seize opportunities from the global clean energy transition. Policies underpinning the target include the Safeguard Mechanism, the Capacity Investment Scheme, and the New Vehicle Efficiency Standard, complemented by programs promoting electrification, renewable energy, and energy efficiency. Australia aims to achieve 82% renewable electricity by 2030 and expand clean energy industries such as hydrogen, green metals, and low-carbon fuels. The plan emphasizes fairness, gender equality, First Nations leadership, and workforce transition through initiatives like the Net Zero Economy Authority and regional workforce strategies. Internationally, Australia supports climate finance, partnerships in the Indo-Pacific, and measures to decarbonize maritime and aviation sectors. The NDC also integrates biodiversity and ocean-based climate solutions, advancing nature repair and blue carbon initiatives.

Angola’s third Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0) reaffirms its commitment to the Paris Agreement and national climate strategies, aiming to strengthen resilience and promote low-carbon development. Covering the period 2025–2035, the NDC integrates climate action into national planning instruments such as the National Climate Change Strategy (ENAC 2022–2035) and the National Development Plan 2023–2027. Its overarching objectives are to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, enhance adaptive capacity, and ensure a just transition that aligns with sustainable development goals while addressing Angola’s high vulnerability to climate change. The NDC sets a dual mitigation target: an unconditional reduction of 5% in GHG emissions by 2035 compared to the 2020 Business-as-Usual (BAU) scenario, and a conditional reduction of up to 11% contingent on international financial, technical, and technological support. Priority measures include expanding renewable energy generation (hydropower and solar), reducing gas flaring in oil fields, promoting energy efficiency, implementing reforestation and assisted natural regeneration, and improving urban waste management through composting and methane capture. These actions aim to deliver measurable climate benefits while generating socio-economic co-benefits such as job creation and improved energy access. Adaptation is a central pillar of Angola’s NDC, reflecting the country’s exposure to droughts, floods, coastal erosion, and biodiversity loss. The plan prioritizes interventions in agriculture, fisheries, water resources, health, coastal zones, and infrastructure to safeguard food security, protect vulnerable livelihoods, and promote ecosystem-based solutions. Actions include strengthening early warning systems, improving water storage and drainage infrastructure, enhancing forest fire prevention, and upgrading health and sanitation systems. Both unconditional and conditional adaptation measures are outlined, with the latter dependent on international support to address Angola’s significant capacity and resource gaps. Effective implementation of the NDC relies on robust governance, institutional coordination, and a strengthened Monitoring, Reporting, and Verification (MRV) system. Angola commits to mobilizing domestic and international finance, leveraging carbon markets, and fostering technology transfer and capacity building. The NDC adopts an inclusive approach that emphasizes gender equality, youth engagement, and community participation, ensuring that climate action contributes to social equity and economic diversification. By aligning climate objectives with national development priorities, Angola seeks to build resilience, reduce emissions, and advance a sustainable, low-carbon future.

The National Climate Finance Strategy 2025–2034 (Estratégia Nacional de Financiamento Climático – ENFC), approved by the Government of Mozambique through Resolution No. 37/2025 of 6 November 2025, establishes a ten-year framework to mobilize, allocate, and manage financial resources for climate change adaptation and mitigation. The strategy aims to strengthen the resilience of Mozambique’s economy, environment, and population to climate-related shocks while promoting sustainable economic development. It seeks to increase access to domestic and international climate finance, improve transparency and efficiency in resource allocation, and align public and private investments with national climate commitments. The strategy is structured around five strategic areas: legal framework reform, fiscal system reform, financial system reform, national capacity building, and access to climate finance. Key interventions include establishing a Mozambique Climate Fund, introducing green budgeting and taxation mechanisms, developing a green investment taxonomy, promoting green bonds and innovative financing instruments, and strengthening access to carbon markets. Particular attention is given to agricultural climate insurance, climate risk financing, forecast-based financing, and decentralized disaster risk management funds to protect vulnerable communities and economic activities from climate-related hazards. Additional measures include strengthening institutional capacities, promoting inclusive green finance, improving monitoring and reporting of climate finance flows, and facilitating debt-for-climate swaps. Implementation is coordinated through a Technical Coordination Council involving ministries responsible for planning, agriculture, environment, finance, health, and other sectors, alongside the Bank of Mozambique and the national disaster management institution.

This National Disaster Risk Management Strategy emphasises the need to establish, streamline, finance, and strengthen disaster risk management (DRM) institutions, coordination frameworks, partnerships, and regulations in Kenya. The overall goal of this Strategy is to effectively implement risk reduction actions within the DRM framework and, most importantly, to integrate DRM into planning and practice, in order to reduce the exposure and vulnerability of communities to hazards while enhancing their capacity to withstand the effects of those hazards. In support of this overall objective, the Strategy identifies five priority areas: the establishment of an institutional and legal framework for DRM; the enhancement of DRM capacities within institutions; disaster information management; strengthening resilience at national, county, and local levels to the impacts of disasters and climate change; mainstreaming disaster risk management into sustainable development policies, strategies, and plans at all levels and across all sectors. This Strategy is structured into seven chapters: 1) chapter one provides an overview of the Kenya National DRM Strategy and the context in which it was developed; 2) chapter 2 gives an overview of Disaster Risk Governance in Kenya, outlining the key components shaping the country’s approach to managing disaster risks; 3) chapter three offers a comprehensive analysis of the current DRM landscape in Kenya, highlighting the roles of various stakeholders; 4) chapter four outlines the guiding principles, strategic objectives, pillars for action, and anticipatory action for DRM; 5) addresses data and knowledge management, with a focus on data collection, processing, sharing, and information exchange; 6) chapter six covers governance and implementation mechanisms, financial resources, budgeting, reserve funds, contingent financing, programme-based risk transfer, and other funding sources; 7) chapter seven focuses on monitoring, evaluation, and learning to ensure sustainability, transparency, accountability, and professionalism at all levels. Concerning strategic pillars and actions for Disaster Risk Management, the Strategy specifies: facilitating development of county-specific DRM legislation and frameworks; supporting county governments to align with national DRM laws and policies; strengthening skills and capacities of DRM personnel and stakeholders; identifying information needs and create platforms for sharing DRM information; strengthening DRM data management and accessibility; promoting interdisciplinary collaboration in research; ensuring development programmes are risk-informed, to reduce vulnerability; documenting, managing and sharing local and indigenous knowledge through a dedicated repository; raising awareness on DRM, including research findings and initiatives; promoting community-driven disaster risk reduction practices; improving early warning system and actions.

policy_description: Programa de Acción Nacional de Lucha contra la Desertificación, Degradación de Tierras y Mitigación de la Sequía (Actualizado a la meta 2030)
policydecision_details: The National Action Programme to Combat Desertification, Land Degradation and Mitigate Drought, Updated to the 2030 Agenda, approved by the Government of Argentina in 2019 through Resolution No. 70/2019, establishes a national framework to prevent and reverse land degradation, combat desertification, and strengthen resilience to drought. The programme aligns national priorities with the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) and the 2030 Agenda, particularly the objective of achieving land degradation neutrality. The programme focuses on sustainable land management, soil conservation, ecosystem restoration, and improved livelihoods in vulnerable rural areas. Its five main components include environmental education and awareness, strengthened policy frameworks and institutional coordination, scientific research and technological innovation, capacity building for local implementation, and mobilization of financial resources. It also promotes participatory approaches involving national and provincial authorities, local communities, research institutions, and the private sector, alongside improved monitoring of land degradation and desertification.

policy_description: AU: Climate Change and Health: Strategic Framework (2025–2029)
policydecision_details: This Africa CDC Climate Change and Health Strategic Framework (2025–2029) provides a roadmap for addressing the growing health impacts of climate change across Africa. It highlights the continent’s vulnerability to climate-related health risks such as vector-borne diseases, waterborne illnesses, food and nutrition insecurity, heat waves, and airborne diseases. The framework emphasizes the One Health approach, integrating human, animal, and environmental health, and sets guiding principles including equity, community engagement, partnerships, and evidence-based interventions. It aims to strengthen health systems, improve disease surveillance, and enhance resilience through governance, capacity building, risk communication, emergency preparedness, research, and innovative financing. The Strategic Framework prioritizes five critical climate-related health vulnerabilities: vector-borne and zoonotic diseases, waterborne diseases, food and nutrition insecurity, heat waves and extreme temperatures, and airborne diseases. To address these, the framework is built on seven strategic pillars: governance and leadership to integrate climate considerations into health policies; capacity building for health professionals and institutions; risk communication and community engagement to raise awareness and foster local participation; public health emergency and disaster response through early warning systems and preparedness; research, innovation, and data for evidence-based interventions; innovative financing to secure sustainable resources; and national health systems strengthening to develop climate-smart infrastructure and stockpile essential medical supplies.

policy_description: Plano Nacional e Desenvolvimento da Bioeconomia (2026-2035)
policydecision_details: The National Bioeconomy Strategy, established by Decree No. 12.044, provides a comprehensive framework for the organization and coordination of activities related to the use of biological resources, scientific knowledge, and innovation. The strategy aims to foster sustainable development by integrating technological processes and knowledge into the national bioeconomy agenda. It mandates the creation of the National Bioeconomy Commission (CNBio), which is tasked with monitoring and supporting the implementation of the strategy. A primary instrument for the execution of this framework is the National Bioeconomy Development Plan (PNDBio), which will serve as the central tool for planning, tracking progress, and monitoring actions over the 2026-2035 period. The scope of the strategy encompasses all economic activities associated with biodiversity and natural resources, ensuring that these are managed in accordance with established national guidelines.
contextoradditionalinfo: The strategy was established to provide a structured approach to the bioeconomy, ensuring that the use of biological resources and biodiversity is aligned with scientific innovation and sustainable development goals.

policy_description: Opinions on Developing New Quality Productive Forces
policydecision_details: The 'Opinions on Developing New Quality Productive Forces' outlines a strategic shift in China's economic policy, emphasizing the role of technological innovation in driving industrial transformation. The framework aims to replace traditional growth drivers with 'new quality productive forces,' which are characterized by high technology, high efficiency, and high quality. It prioritizes the integration of digital technologies with traditional industries, the development of strategic emerging industries, and the cultivation of future-oriented sectors. The policy mandates the optimization of resource allocation to support innovation, the strengthening of talent development, and the creation of a favorable institutional environment for scientific and technological breakthroughs. While the scope is national and cross-sectoral, it implicitly impacts the modernization of the agricultural sector through the promotion of smart agriculture and advanced agrifood technologies.
contextoradditionalinfo: The strategy is designed to address the growing domestic demand for dairy products in Viet Nam, reduce reliance on imports, and improve the efficiency and sustainability of the national livestock sector.

policydecision_details: Thailand’s National Biodiversity Action Plan 2023–2027 establishes a five-year framework to conserve and restore biodiversity, promote sustainable use of biological resources and integrate biodiversity considerations into national and sectoral development policies, in alignment with the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework and the Sustainable Development Goals. The plan identifies three strategic priorities and 12 national biodiversity targets, addressing ecosystem conservation and restoration, sustainable bioeconomic development, and institutional capacity and participation. Key quantitative objectives include expanding protected and conserved areas to at least 30% of the country’s territory by 2030, developing at least five local biodiversity management plans, and increasing biodiversity information disclosure to at least 20%. Priority measures include expanding protected areas and other effective area-based conservation measures (OECMs), restoring degraded ecosystems, protecting threatened species, managing invasive alien species, promoting sustainable agriculture, fisheries, forestry and tourism, and strengthening access and benefit-sharing mechanisms for genetic resources. Implementation covers 2023–2027, coordinated by the Office of Natural Resources and Environmental Policy and Planning, with participation from government agencies, local communities, businesses and research institutions. The plan establishes monitoring and evaluation mechanisms and promotes domestic and international biodiversity financing, without specifying a single consolidated implementation budget in its executive summary.

policy_description: Ireland’s Long-term Strategy on Greenhouse Gas Emissions Reduction 2024
policydecision_details: Ireland’s Long-term Strategy on Greenhouse Gas Emissions Reduction (2024) establishes a national roadmap to achieve a climate-neutral, climate-resilient, biodiversity-rich and environmentally sustainable economy by 2050. It builds on the legally binding target of reducing greenhouse gas emissions by 51% by 2030 compared with 2018 levels, supported by national carbon budgets and sectoral emissions ceilings. Priority measures include expanding renewable electricity, improving energy efficiency, decarbonizing transport and industry, reducing agricultural methane and nitrous oxide emissions, restoring peatlands, promoting sustainable forestry and strengthening carbon sequestration. The strategy also emphasizes circular economy development, climate adaptation, citizen engagement and a just transition. Implementation extends through 2050, guided by annual Climate Action Plans, sector-specific policies and investment programmes. Progress is monitored through national carbon budgeting and emissions reporting, with the strategy scheduled for review and updating no later than 2029. It discusses investment requirements but does not establish a single consolidated implementation budget.

policy_description: Third National Communication To the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change
policydecision_details: Guyana’s Third National Communication (2024) provides a comprehensive assessment of the country’s greenhouse gas emissions, climate vulnerabilities, mitigation and adaptation measures, and climate finance requirements under the UNFCCC. It presents an updated national greenhouse gas inventory covering 1990–2016 and assesses mitigation opportunities in energy, transport, agriculture, forestry and land use. Particular emphasis is placed on forest conservation, REDD+, renewable energy development and the Low Carbon Development Strategy 2030, alongside adaptation priorities addressing coastal flooding, water management, climate-resilient agriculture, biodiversity protection and infrastructure resilience. The report also examines climate finance received, technology transfer, institutional capacity and monitoring systems, identifying financial and technical constraints to implementation. It supports national climate planning and international reporting obligations but does not establish a new implementation period, consolidated budget or independent quantitative emissions reduction targets, as it primarily documents existing policies, climate risks and progress towards national commitments.

Nigeria’s Long-Term Low-Emission Development Strategy (LT-LEDS) establishes a national roadmap to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2060, while promoting climate-resilient economic development, energy security and sustainable growth. It builds on the country’s 2021 NDC, which targets a 47% reduction in emissions by 2030 compared with business-as-usual, conditional on international support. Priority measures cover agriculture, forestry and land use, energy, transport, buildings, industry, oil and gas, and waste management. Key interventions include renewable energy expansion, clean cooking, sustainable transport, methane emissions reduction, climate-smart agriculture, afforestation, ecosystem restoration and improved forest management. Adaptation priorities address food security, water resources, infrastructure resilience and climate-related disasters. Implementation extends through 2060, coordinated by the National Council on Climate Change and supported by sectoral action plans, international cooperation and monitoring mechanisms. The strategy identifies approximately USD 859 billion in cumulative international financial support requirements under its ambitious renewable energy scenario, while Nigeria’s broader Energy Transition Plan estimates investment needs of USD 1.9 trillion. A dedicated LT-LEDS financing strategy remains to be developed.

Türkiye’s Long-Term Climate Strategy, approved on 4 November 2024, establishes a comprehensive national roadmap to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2053, supporting sustainable economic development, climate resilience and a transition towards a low-carbon economy. It builds on Türkiye’s updated 2023 Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC), which targets a 41% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 compared with the business-as-usual scenario, corresponding to an emissions level of approximately 695 MtCO₂e. The strategy comprises 89 strategies across 18 sectors and four cross-cutting areas, including 35 mitigation strategies, 38 adaptation strategies and 16 strategies addressing technology, just transition, climate finance and capacity building. Priority measures include renewable energy expansion, industrial decarbonization, energy efficiency, sustainable transportation, circular economy practices and improved waste management. In agriculture and land use, the strategy emphasizes climate-smart agriculture, sustainable livestock management, efficient fertilizer use, water conservation, forest restoration, biodiversity protection and enhanced carbon sequestration. Adaptation priorities address water scarcity, drought, extreme weather, ecosystem degradation, agricultural vulnerability and disaster risk reduction. Implementation extends through 2053, supported by the Climate Change Mitigation and Adaptation Strategies and Action Plans (2024–2030), carbon pricing mechanisms, green finance and institutional coordination. The strategy does not establish a single consolidated implementation budget, instead identifying financing mechanisms and long-term sectoral priorities to support the transition.

Spain’s National Climate Change Adaptation Plan (PNACC) 2021–2030, approved on 22 September 2020 and submitted to the UNFCCC in December 2024, establishes a comprehensive national framework to reduce vulnerability to climate change, strengthen the resilience of ecosystems and socioeconomic sectors, and integrate adaptation into public policies and development planning. The plan identifies 18 priority areas and 81 sectoral lines of action, addressing water resources, agriculture, livestock and food security, biodiversity, forestry, desertification, coastal and marine ecosystems, human health, infrastructure, energy and tourism. Priority measures include improving climate risk assessments and early warning systems, promoting climate-resilient agriculture and sustainable water management, restoring degraded ecosystems, protecting biodiversity, strengthening forest resilience against wildfires and adapting coastal infrastructure to rising sea levels. Implementation covers 2021–2030, structured around two five-year work programmes. The first programme (2021–2025) includes 257 measures and 11 sub-measures, with responsibilities distributed among national, regional and local authorities. The plan also establishes monitoring indicators, periodic evaluations and mechanisms for stakeholder participation and institutional coordination. It does not establish a single consolidated implementation budget or overarching quantitative adaptation outcome targets, relying instead on sectoral programmes, public financing instruments and European Union funding mechanisms.

Norway’s updated National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan (NBSAP), adopted on 27 September 2024, establishes a national framework to halt biodiversity loss, promote sustainable use of natural resources and strengthen ecosystem resilience, aligning national policies with the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework and its 23 global targets for 2030. Key national objectives include conserving 30% of Norway’s terrestrial areas by 2030 through protected areas and other effective area-based conservation measures, reducing the conversion of particularly important natural areas by 2030, and minimizing their net loss by 2050. The strategy also aims to identify the extent of degraded ecosystems and increase ecological restoration efforts, without establishing a separate quantified national restoration target. Priority measures include sustainable land-use planning, forest and wetland restoration, biodiversity-friendly agriculture, sustainable forestry and fisheries, invasive species management, ecosystem accounting and stronger integration of biodiversity into sectoral policies. Implementation follows the 2030 and 2050 horizons, involving national authorities, municipalities, businesses and local communities, with comprehensive progress assessments every four years. The plan does not establish a consolidated implementation budget, relying on existing and future public financing arrangements and sectoral instruments.

policy_description: Plan de Acción de Biodiversidad de Colombia al 2030
policydecision_details: Colombia’s National Biodiversity Action Plan 2024–2030 aims to halt biodiversity loss, restore degraded ecosystems and promote sustainable, inclusive economic development, aligning national priorities with the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. It establishes four strategic priorities, six national targets and 191 commitments, addressing ecosystem conservation, sustainable production, biodiversity-based economic development, pollution reduction, environmental governance and financing. Key targets by 2030 include integrating at least 19 million hectares into territorial planning with biodiversity and climate adaptation criteria, maintaining an ecological restoration rate of at least 75,000 hectares annually after 2026, and mobilizing COP 22.5 trillion in biodiversity financing. Implementation covers 2024–2030, involving national ministries, regional authorities, Indigenous Peoples, local communities and private-sector stakeholders. The estimated implementation cost is approximately COP 76.5 trillion (USD 19.4 billion) over seven years, supported by public and private financing, international cooperation and monitoring mechanisms

The Policy Statement is a government document that provides clear strategic direction to guide Eswatini toward achieving developed-country status by 2030. The nation’s vision is to transition from a lower-middle-income to a high-income country. Specifically, the Government envisions “A well-developed, inclusive, peaceful, stable, and economically prosperous Kingdom of Eswatini, grounded in cultural values and ensuring the well-being of all emaSwati.” Aligned with the National Development Strategy and Plan, the Mission of the Government of the Kingdom of Eswatini is to provide leadership and drive the implementation of comprehensive strategies and programs aimed at transforming the economy. The Policy Statement provides general directions, which include (i) achieving high-income, developed country status by 2030; (ii) promoting economic transformation, poverty reduction, and enhanced governance, in particular promoting industrialization and supporting mega investments and growth in key sectors such as infrastructure, agriculture, manufacturing, and services; (iii) fostering investment, innovation, and inclusive growth.
